rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: NEB-style practice beyond the verified PYQs recorded on the parent canonicals.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Two independent checks - perpendicularity and equidistance - close every bisector computation.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The factor 2*** - sqrt20 = 2sqrt5: the unequal normalisers put a 2 into the bisector equation; dropping it produces lines that are not bisectors at all.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The worked example is four named theorems in sequence - each step consumes a licence, none is mere arithmetic.  ·  Pipeline: standardise (c > 0), normalise (divide by sqrt(a^2+b^2)), rule (a1a2 + b1b2), both bisectors, perpendicularity check. Unequal normalisers: multiply through by the lcm before expanding - the factor 2 from sqrt20 = 2sqrt5 is the classic drop. Verify twice: slopes product -1, and equidistance at a bisector point. Negative dot product under the convention means the same-side (+) wedge is the acute one.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Angle Bisector Worked Example (the a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ Method at Full Speed) This canonical runs the **complete bisector computation on one concrete pair**: the lines x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0, from normalisation through the acute/obtuse verdict to the finished equations. It is the worked-example face of the rule canonical.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror (as used in the example) - **Standardise:** both constants made positive — L₁: −x − 2y + 5 = 0 (a₁ = −1, b₁ = −2), L₂: 4x + 2y + 9 = 0 (a₂ = 4, b₂ = 2). - **Normalisers:** √5 and √20 = 2√5. - **Rule:** a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = (−1)(4) + (−2)(2) = **−8 < 0** ⟹ the (+) bisector is **acute**, the (−) bisector obtuse.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Clear the normalisers' lcm first; then the ± expansion is plain integer algebra.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (6m): Find the equations of the bisectors of the angles between x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0, and label the acute one.** — **Standardise:** L₁ ⟹ −x − 2y + 5 = 0 (c = 5 > 0); L₂ already has c = 9 > 0. **Normalisers:** √5 and √(16+4) = √20 = 2√5.…  ·  **NEB-style (5m): Verify that the point (1/6, 0) lies on the acute bisector 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 and is equidistant from the two lines.** — **On the bisector:** 6(1/6) + 0 − 1 = 0 ✓. **Distance to L₁ (x+2y−5=0):** |1/6 + 0 − 5|/√5 = |−29/6|/√5 = 29/(6√5). **Distance to L₂ (4x+2y+9=0):** |4/6 + 0 + 9|/√20 = |29/3 + 9|...…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Narrate the rule's verdict in a sentence - the classification mark lives in the reasoning, not the sign.

rows.text: Angle-bisector formulas at a glance · Form | Statement | When to use · Distance form | $\dfrac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{√(a_1²+b_1²)} = ±\dfrac{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}{√(a_2²+b_2²)}$ | always works; pick signs by region · Same-side check | same sign for both lines on one side | chooses the internal/external branch · Slope form | $\tanθ = \dfrac{m_2−m_1}{1+m_1m_2}$ with $\tanθ = \tan(\952;/2)$ | quick check for the…  ·  Worked example sign map · Region | Sign of L₁ | Sign of L₂ | Bisector equation · Inside the acute angle | + | + | use both with + · Outside L₁ side | − | + | flip the first sign · Outside L₂ side | + | − | flip the second sign · Opposite the origin | − | − | both negative again

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The verdict -8 < 0 was predictable: opposing normals sandwich the acute wedge on the same-side equation.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (5m): Without computing the bisectors, determine which of the (+)/(−) bisectors of x + 2y − 5 = 0 and 4x + 2y + 9 = 0 is acute, and justify.** — **Standardise:** L₁ ⟹ −x−2y+5 = 0 (a₁ = −1, b₁ = −2); L₂: a₂ = 4, b₂ = 2. **Dot product:** a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = −4 − 4 = **−8 < 0**.…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): The bisectors of two lines are 6x + 6y − 1 = 0 and 2x − 2y + 19 = 0. Find the angle between the bisectors and comment on what it verifies.** — **Slopes:** m₁ = −1, m₂ = 1. **Angle:** tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| = |2/(1 − 1)| = 2/0 ⟹ θ = **90°**.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — Reading the Example as a Chain of Licences - Each step consumes a theorem: the standardisation licenses the rule, the normalisers convert equations into distances, the dot-product verdict assigns the labels, and the perpendicularity closes the audit.…  ·  ## 4. Deep Conceptual — Why the Verdict (−8 < 0) Was Predictable - The normals (−1, −2) and (4, 2) point in *opposing* half-plane directions (dot product negative) — the same-side wedge (the (+) equation) is the narrow one.…  ·  ## 5. Worked Example Types - **Type A — full pipeline:** standardise → normalise → rule → both bisectors → checks. - **Type B — factor discipline:** unequal normalisers, lcm multiplication. - **Type C — definition check:** equidistance verified at a bisector point.…
